title: What Colorado's Latest Municipal Election Results Mean for Local Taxes and Community Projects - NewsBreak
text:
3 minutes ago On November 4, 2025, voters in at least 67 cities and towns in Colorado participated in municipal elections. They voted on local candidates and ballot measures. Of these, 43 were regular elections and 23 were special elections. Voters considered 138 municipal ballot issues and questions statewide. Five municipalities canceled their regular elections this year. The reported results are unofficial and may change as final counts are confirmed.
Many ballot measures addressed tax issues, especially sales and use tax increases. Several municipalities approved these increases for specific purposes. Aspen passed a tax to support the local school district. Evans approved a tax for street maintenance. Fort Morgan passed a tax for an aquatics center. Merino approved a tax for health and safety. Pagosa Springs passed a tax for sewage and wastewater facilities. Timnath approved a tax for a recreation center. Westminster passed a tax for emergency services and street improvements. Similar tax proposals did not pass in Ault, Bayfield, Hot Sulphur Springs, Kiowa, Mead, Pueblo, Sterling, and Walsenburg. In these places, voters rejected increases for community services, infrastructure, and law enforcement.
Some cities also voted on extending existing sales and use taxes. Boulder voters approved an extension of the community, culture, resilience, and safety (CCRS) tax for capital projects. Cañon City, Florence, Fort Collins, Fort Lupton, Pueblo, and Trinidad passed various extensions to fund street infrastructure, water acquisition, economic development, and public works. Fort Collins also approved a measure to extend the Open Space Sales and Use Tax with changes.
Lodging and short-term rental taxes were also on the ballot. Basalt, Kiowa, and Mountain View passed new or increased lodging taxes to fund workforce housing, infrastructure, and other municipal purposes. Similar measures did not pass in Bayfield, Rifle, Severance, and Vail. In these cities, the proposed taxes were intended to support housing, visitor improvements, and public safety.
Voters in Durango, Gunnison, and Rico approved property tax mill levy increases. These increases will fund fire protection, emergency services, and street maintenance. Other tax and fee proposals, such as an excise tax in Cañon City and an ordinance in Louisville, were not approved. The election results show a range of local priorities and fiscal strategies as Colorado municipalities address community needs and plan for future development.
